paper_a.title: Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning

metadata.description: DQN (Mnih et al. 2013) extends NFQ (Riedmiller 2005). Both train a neural network to approximate the Q-function by minimising a squared TD loss against bootstrapped targets. NFQ does this in batch mode with Rprop on a fixed sample set D; DQN replaces the batch Rprop fit with online stochastic gradient descent (RMSProp) over a sliding-window experience-replay buffer, scaling to high-dimensional pixel inputs via a CNN and applying it to Atari. The DQN paper explicitly cites NFQ as the closest prior work (AP238.3 in the DQN extraction directly references the NFQ algorithm).

matches.explanation: Both are model-free optimal-control problems on an unknown MDP. NFQ poses generic continuous-state control of an MDP minimising cumulated costs; DQN narrows the same template to learning Atari-game policies from raw $210 \times 160$ RGB pixels with reward signals. Same mathematical role (the top-level problem each algorithm solves) but very different domains.

NFQ's MDP definition (states $S$, actions $A$, transitions $p$, costs $c$) is the standard textbook MDP. DQN splits the same content into two paper-origin definitions: agent-environment interaction with action set $\mathcal{A}=\{1,\ldots,K\}$, observations $x_t$, and rewards $r_t$; plus a state-sequence definition $s_t = x_1,a_1,\ldots,x_t$ that handles partial observability. NFQ assumes states are observable, so DQN's state-sequence construction is an extension; the underlying MDP framework is the same.

DQN explicitly defines the discounted return $R_t = \sum_{t'=t}^T \gamma^{t'-t} r_{t'}$. NFQ refers to 'expected cumulated (discounted) costs' inside its problem statement but does not isolate the return as a separate definition. Conceptually present in NFQ's framing but no node-level counterpart in the JSON.

DQN defines $Q^*(s,a) = \max_\pi \mathbb{E}[R_t \mid s_t=s, a_t=a, \pi]$ as a separate optimal action-value-function definition. NFQ uses $Q$ throughout (its update rule EP239.1 and target rule EP239.3 both invoke $\min_b Q_k(s',b)$) but does not give the optimal $Q^*$ a standalone definition node. Conceptually understood as standard background in NFQ; not present as a node.

DQN's `Q-Network' definition $Q(s,a;\theta) \approx Q^*(s,a)$ as a CNN-parametrised approximator does not have a matching standalone definition in NFQ — NFQ folds the MLP-as-Q-approximator idea directly into the algorithm node AP239.4 and its training equation EP239.2 rather than giving the parametrised Q-function its own definition.

DQN defines $\rho(s,a)$, the behaviour distribution from which off-policy samples are drawn. NFQ uses a sample set $D$ collected under unspecified (random or greedy-exploit) policies but does not formalise a behaviour distribution — RP239.2 mentions a greedy-exploit collection variant in passing. No node-level counterpart.

Both define a stored sample buffer of transitions used to train the Q-network. NFQ's `Sample Set $D$' stores triples $(s,a,s')$ pooled across interactions and is reused every outer iteration in batch fashion; DQN's `Experience Replay Memory' stores $(s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1})$ in a fixed-capacity ring of size $N$ from which random minibatches are drawn for online SGD updates. Same conceptual object (replay/sample buffer) — DQN extends with sliding-window capacity and minibatching.

DQN's preprocessing function $\phi$ (gray-scale, downsample to $110\times 84$, crop to $84\times 84$, stack 4 frames) is specific to high-dimensional image inputs and has no analogue in NFQ, whose benchmarks (pole-balancing, mountain car, cartpole) work directly on low-dimensional state vectors.

DQN's specific CNN architecture (conv 16 $8\times 8$/4 + ReLU, conv 32 $4\times 4$/2 + ReLU, FC 256 ReLU, one linear output per action) is paper-original and a key contribution. NFQ uses small fully-connected MLPs (3-5-5-1, 5-5-5-1) appropriate to its low-dimensional benchmarks; the architectures are not comparable.

Same squared-TD loss for training a neural Q-function. NFQ writes $\mathrm{error} = (Q(s,a) - (c(s,a) + \gamma \min_b Q(s',b)))^2$ (cost-minimisation convention), DQN writes $L_i(\theta_i) = \mathbb{E}[(y_i - Q(s,a;\theta_i))^2]$ with $y_i = \mathbb{E}[r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s',a';\theta_{i-1}) \mid s,a]$ (reward-maximisation convention with explicit expectations over $\rho$ and $\mathcal{E}$). Identical objective up to sign convention and explicit expectation; DQN extras (prior-iterate target $\theta_{i-1}$, behaviour distribution $\rho$) are minor formalisations of what NFQ does informally with $Q_k$.

DQN explicitly writes the gradient of the Q-learning loss $\nabla_{\theta_i} L_i = \mathbb{E}[(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s',a';\theta_{i-1}) - Q(s,a;\theta_i)) \nabla_{\theta_i} Q(s,a;\theta_i)]$ as a standalone equation. NFQ does not isolate the gradient (Rprop hides it inside the supervised batch trainer), so no node-level counterpart.

Core algorithm match. Both train a neural Q-function by repeatedly fitting it to bootstrapped TD targets computed from a current iterate $Q_k$ over a stored set of transitions. NFQ does this fully batch: each outer iteration k regenerates the entire pattern set from $D$ and re-fits the MLP to convergence with Rprop. DQN does it online: at each environment step, sample a random minibatch from the replay buffer $\mathcal{D}$ and take a single SGD step (RMSProp) on the squared TD error, with the previous parameter snapshot $\theta_{i-1}$ playing the role of $Q_k$. Same fitted-Q-iteration template; DQN extends with online SGD, sliding-window replay, $\epsilon$-greedy on-line data collection, frame-skipping, and CNN scale. The DQN paper's own AP238.3 node explicitly cites NFQ as the closest prior method.

DQN's external-origin node `Neural Fitted Q-learning (NFQ)' (cited as Riedmiller 2005, RPROP-based batch Q-learning) refers to exactly the algorithm that is the paper-origin contribution AP239.4 in paper B. This is a `paper-A external citation matches paper-B contribution' alignment, which is direct evidence for relation_type=EXT.

Both papers cite an adaptive per-parameter gradient method to train the MLP Q-function. NFQ uses Rprop (Riedmiller & Braun 1993), which is a batch supervised trainer adapting per-weight step sizes by sign of the partial derivative. DQN uses RMSProp (Tieleman & Hinton), an online minibatch adaptive-learning-rate method conceptually descended from Rprop (RMSProp = `Rprop adapted for stochastic minibatches'). Both are externally cited; aligned because their role in each pipeline is the same (Q-network optimiser).

Both are externally cited tabular Q-learning (Watkins 1989 / Sutton & Barto 1998). Same algorithm; this match carries no information about the A↔B relationship per the prompt's origin-aware filtering rule, but is included for completeness as both papers ground their method in classical Q-learning.

Externally cited Bellman-equation / classical Q-learning update. DQN gives the Bellman equation in expectation form $Q^*(s,a) = \mathbb{E}_{s'}[r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^*(s',a')]$; NFQ gives the corresponding tabular sample update $Q_{k+1}(s,a) := (1-\alpha)Q(s,a) + \alpha(c(s,a) + \gamma \min_b Q_k(s',b))$. Same canonical fixed-point/contraction at the heart of Q-learning, both attributed to Sutton & Barto.

NFQ defines `optimal policy' $\pi^*: S \to A$ as the cost-minimising state-to-action map, with the side conditions $S$ continuous, $A$ finite, $p$ unknown (model-free). DQN never defines policy as a node — it works directly with $Q^*$ and the implied greedy/$\epsilon$-greedy policy. Conceptually present in DQN's $\epsilon$-greedy machinery but not as a standalone definition.

NFQ's goal-state set $S^+$ and forbidden-state set $S^-$ are core to its cost-shaping target rule (EP239.3) for reaching/avoidance/regulator tasks on low-dimensional benchmarks. DQN uses dense per-frame rewards from the Atari emulator with $\{-1,0,+1\}$ clipping (RP238.2) — there are no goal/forbidden state regions in its formulation.

NFQ's `working region' definition (single starting state vs finite set vs random within a region) reflects its control-theory framing where the controller is judged from a designated set of initial conditions. DQN evaluates by full-game playthroughs starting from the emulator's natural initial state; no working-region concept appears.

NFQ's taxonomy of control tasks (avoidance / goal-reaching / regulator) is specific to its low-dimensional benchmarks and the cost-shaping in EP239.3. DQN's Atari setting does not fit this taxonomy — the games provide intrinsic dense reward rather than goal/forbidden regions.

NFQ's per-sample target rule with special cases for $S^+$ (target $= c(s,u,s')$) and $S^-$ (target $= C^-$, set to $1.0$ to match the MLP output range) implements goal/forbidden cost shaping. DQN has only the standard terminal vs non-terminal split inside ASP238.6 ($y_j = r_j$ if terminal, else $y_j = r_j + \gamma \max_{a'} Q$); no $S^+/S^-$ shaping.

NFQ's `Online Neural Q-Learning' is the per-sample-backprop strawman it argues against (cited as suffering from interference and slow learning). DQN does not isolate this strawman as its own algorithm node — the closest analogue would be AP238.2 itself (DQN updates online but with replay-buffer minibatches), which is already aligned with NFQ's main algorithm AP239.4.
